title: Christmas Ham EVERYONE Makes WRONG (Why Yours Is DRY and SALTY)

scenes.text: Sweetheart, on Christmas Day in our house, the ham came out of the oven shining like stained glass. Dark amber glaze, a diamond pattern cut into the top, and a clove in the middle of every diamond. My father carried it to the table on my grandmother's blue platter like he was carrying the crown jewels. And the whole family clapped. Every year.
scenes.caption: LIKE STAINED GLASS

scenes.text: But today, people tell me their Christmas ham comes out dry and stringy, or so salty you need a pitcher of water, or the glaze burns black. So tonight I'm giving you my brown sugar glazed ham, every step, and the five mistakes that make it dry and salty. And stay with me, because the last trick is when to put on the glaze, and it's the reason most glazes burn.
scenes.caption: DRY AND SALTY

scenes.text: Ham at Christmas is an old tradition, honey, older than America. In the old days, farm families butchered a hog in late fall, and salted and smoked the hams to keep through the winter. The best ham was saved for Christmas. On Grandma Pearl's farm, the hams hung in the smokehouse from November, and on Christmas Eve, my grandfather would take one down like he was picking the best apple.
scenes.caption: THE SMOKEHOUSE

scenes.text: By the time I was cooking, in the sixties, everybody bought their ham at the grocery store, already cooked and smoked. That's what most hams are today. And that changes everything about how you cook it, because you're not really cooking it, honey. You're only warming it, and glazing it. In a minute I'll tell you why that's the secret to a juicy ham.
scenes.caption: YOU'RE ONLY WARMING IT

scenes.text: And my mother's Christmas ham was the one dinner she never let anybody help with. She'd shoo us all out of the kitchen on Christmas morning, while we played with our presents. Danny and I would sneak to the kitchen door and smell it through the crack. Brown sugar, cloves, and smoke. To this day, that smell means Christmas to me more than any tree or any carol.
scenes.caption: THROUGH THE CRACK

scenes.text: First, choosing the ham. Look for a fully cooked, bone-in ham, either a shank end or a butt end, eight to ten pounds. That feeds twelve people with leftovers. Bone-in is juicier and has more flavor than boneless, and you get the bone for soup afterward. My mother always said, the bone is the best part of the ham, and the soup is the best part of New Year's.
scenes.caption: BONE-IN

scenes.text: And here's mistake number one. Buying a ham with water added. Read the label, sweetheart. If it says ham with natural juices, that's good. If it says ham, water added, or ham and water product, it's been pumped full of salty water. It shrinks in the oven, tastes like salt, and the texture is spongy. Pay the extra dollar for a better ham.
scenes.caption: READ THE LABEL

scenes.text: And spiral-cut hams are easy, but they dry out the fastest, because all those slices let the juice out. If you buy one, cook it face down, wrapped tight in foil, and watch it closely. I like a whole ham that I score myself. It stays juicier, and it looks prettier on the table. That's how my father liked it.
scenes.caption: SPIRAL HAMS DRY OUT

scenes.text: Step one. Take the ham out of the icebox two hours before it goes in the oven, so it warms up a little. Mistake number two is putting an ice-cold ham in the oven. The outside dries out while you wait for the middle to warm up. Heat the oven to three hundred twenty-five. Not hotter.
scenes.caption: TWO HOURS OUT

scenes.text: Step two, scoring. With a sharp knife, cut a diamond pattern into the fat on top, about a quarter of an inch deep. Cut lines one inch apart in one direction, and then the other way, across them. Don't cut too deep into the meat. Then press a whole clove into the middle of each diamond. The cuts let the glaze sink in, and the cloves make it smell like Christmas.
scenes.caption: A DIAMOND PATTERN

scenes.text: Step three. Put the ham, cut side down, in a roasting pan. Pour about a cup of water or apple juice into the bottom of the pan. Then cover the whole pan tightly with foil. Mistake number three is roasting it uncovered at a high heat. The foil keeps the steam in, and the steam keeps the ham juicy while it warms.
scenes.caption: COVER IT TIGHT

scenes.text: If this is helping you, honey, tap the like button for me. It helps Grandma more than you know. Now, bake it at three twenty-five for about twelve to fifteen minutes per pound. An eight pound ham takes about an hour and forty-five minutes to two hours. But use a thermometer, like I always say. A fully cooked ham only needs to reach one hundred forty degrees in the middle.
scenes.caption: ONE HUNDRED FORTY

scenes.text: And here's mistake number four, the one that makes it dry and stringy. Cooking it too long, until it's one sixty or one seventy, like a fresh pork roast. Remember, it's already cooked. You're only warming it. Once it's past one forty, every minute in the oven squeezes out more juice. Take it out at one thirty, glaze it, and it'll be one forty when it's done.
scenes.caption: IT'S ALREADY COOKED

scenes.text: Now the glaze. While the ham warms, make it in a small saucepan. One cup of packed brown sugar. A quarter cup of honey. Two tablespoons of Dijon or spicy brown mustard. Two tablespoons of orange juice or pineapple juice. A pinch of ground cloves and cinnamon. Stir it over low heat for three or four minutes until it's smooth and bubbling.
scenes.caption: THE GLAZE

scenes.text: The mustard is the secret, honey. It cuts through the sweetness and the salt, so the glaze doesn't taste like candy. My mother used a spoon of her own pickle juice from the cellar, too. And for a Christmas twist, add two tablespoons of bourbon. My husband said that ham was the only reason he went to church that year.
scenes.caption: THE MUSTARD IS THE SECRET

scenes.text: So far, a bone-in ham with natural juices, out of the icebox early, scored and studded with cloves, covered tight with foil, low and slow, and only to one forty. Now the trick I promised, about when to put on the glaze. Mistake number five is glazing the ham at the start. Sugar can't take two hours in the oven. It burns black and bitter, and it smokes up your kitchen.
scenes.caption: IT BURNS BLACK

scenes.text: Here's how. When the ham reaches one hundred thirty degrees, take it out and turn the oven up to four hundred. Take off the foil. Brush half the glaze all over the top and sides, into all the cuts. Put it back in, uncovered, for ten minutes. Then brush on the rest of the glaze, and give it ten more minutes, until it's bubbling and shiny and dark amber.
scenes.caption: THE LAST TWENTY MINUTES

scenes.text: Watch it closely those last minutes, sweetheart. Sugar goes from beautiful to burnt very fast. If the edges get too dark, lay a little foil over them. And spoon the drippings from the pan over the ham once or twice. That's what gives it that stained glass shine my father carried to the table.
scenes.caption: WATCH IT CLOSELY

scenes.text: And here's an old trick for a fancier ham, honey, the one from the magazines in nineteen sixty. Pin pineapple rings all over the ham with toothpicks before the last glaze, with a maraschino cherry in the middle of each ring. It looks like a party. My granddaughter thinks it's the silliest thing she ever saw, and she asks for it every year.
scenes.caption: LIKE A PARTY

scenes.text: Let it rest twenty minutes, covered loosely with foil, before you carve, so the juices settle. To carve, cut along the bone to take off big pieces, then slice each piece across the grain, thin. Put the slices on a warm platter, and spoon the pan juices and any extra glaze over them. Nobody ever needs a glass of water at my table.
scenes.caption: SLICE IT THIN

scenes.text: And serve it the old Ohio way, honey. Scalloped potatoes, green beans, a jar of my mother's spiced peaches, and warm rolls with butter. And a little bowl of spicy brown mustard on the side for the men. My father put mustard on everything. My mother said he'd put it on the Christmas pie if she let him.
scenes.caption: THE OLD OHIO WAY

scenes.text: Leftover ham keeps five days in the icebox, and freezes for two months, wrapped tight. Ham sandwiches on Boxing Day. Ham and eggs on Sunday. Ham and cheese in a casserole. And save that bone, sweetheart. Put it in a big pot with a pound of dried split peas or navy beans, an onion and a carrot, and simmer it for three hours. That's the best soup of the whole year.
scenes.query: ham bone split pea soup pot
scenes.caption: SAVE THAT BONE

scenes.text: So one more time. Bone-in ham, with natural juices, no water added. Out of the icebox two hours early. Score it, clove it. Cut side down, a cup of juice, covered tight. Three twenty-five, only to one thirty. Then the glaze, in two coats, the last twenty minutes, at four hundred. Rest it, and slice it thin. That's a Christmas ham that's never dry and never salty.
scenes.caption: NEVER DRY

scenes.text: Tell me in the comments, sweetheart. Ham or turkey for Christmas dinner at your house? Or both, like mine? The whole playlist of Grandma's recipes is right there on your screen, and I'll see you in the next video. Good night, honey. Merry Christmas.
scenes.caption: HAM OR TURKEY?
